questions.q: What changes when a unique clustered index is created on a view?
options: SQL Server materializes the view — physically storing the computed result on disk, like a table
The view's SELECT statement is deleted
Nothing changes functionally, only performance improves slightly
The view becomes read-only permanently
questions.explain: This is the one case where a view genuinely stores data, contradicting the general rule from Lesson 58.

questions.q: What is the ongoing cost of an indexed view?
options: SQL Server must update the stored data every time the underlying table changes (INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE)
Indexed views cannot be queried at all
They require manual refresh commands run daily
There is no cost — indexed views are strictly better than regular views
questions.explain: Faster reads come at the cost of extra write-time maintenance work to keep the materialized data consistent.

questions.q: What does WITH SCHEMABINDING do, and why is it required for indexed views?
options: It locks the underlying table's structure so SQL Server can guarantee the view stays valid
It hides the view from Object Explorer
It automatically creates the clustered index
It converts the view into a stored procedure
questions.explain: SCHEMABINDING prevents structural changes to underlying tables that would break the materialized view.

questions.q: Which aggregate function must be used in place of COUNT(*) in an indexed view?
options: COUNT_BIG(*)
SUM(*)
COUNT_LARGE(*)
TOTAL(*)
questions.explain: This is one of several real syntax restrictions specific to indexed view definitions.

questions.q: When does an indexed view make the most sense?
options: For expensive aggregations, queried very often, on data that doesn't change constantly
For every view in a database, without exception
Only for views with fewer than 10 rows
Only when the underlying table changes constantly
questions.explain: This is the classic reporting/dashboard-summary profile — for most everyday views, a regular view is simpler and sufficient.
